slides.title: Keeping Time with the Skies
slides.subtitle: At the Patang Mahotsav in Ahmedabad, Meera spots the Moon shining in broad daylight — and starts wondering how the sky has always kept our time.
points: Have you ever seen the Moon during the day — why is it sometimes visible when the Sun is up?
If you lived on the Moon instead of Earth, what would a day, a month, or a year even mean?
If we had no clocks or calendars, how else could we measure the passing of time?

slides.title: A Moon in the daytime sky
slides.body: Meera always thought the Moon came out only at night. Yet here it was over the kites — and not a full circle, but a thin slice. She knew the Moon is **spherical** and shines by **reflecting sunlight**, so why isn't the whole Moon visible every night? For a moment she wondered about a **lunar eclipse** — but eclipses are rare and brief. So what really makes the Moon change shape?

slides.title: How does the Moon's appearance change and why?
slides.intro: Let us watch the Moon carefully over a month to understand how its appearance changes — beginning at sunrise after a full Moon, when it is easiest to spot.

slides.title: Track the Moon for a whole month
slides.purpose: The Moon's shape *seems* to change night after night. To find the pattern, we record it ourselves — best begun a month or more before this chapter is taught.
steps: Spot — find the Moon at sunrise in the western direction the first day after the full Moon
Record — in a table like Table 11.1, note the date, whether you saw it at sunrise or sunset, and shade a circle to show the bright portion
Compare — from day two, note whether the bright part is increasing or decreasing, and whether the Moon is closer to or farther from the Sun than the day before
slides.observe: The bright portion **shrinks day by day**, and the Moon drifts **closer to the Sun**. After about 15 days it vanishes from the morning sky — so for the next 15 days you watch at **sunset** instead, where the bright part grows back.

slides.title: Phases of the Moon
slides.intro: From a full bright circle to nothing and back — the changing shapes have names, and a rhythm.

slides.title: Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha
slides.body: The bright part shrinks from a full circle to nothing over about two weeks — the **waning** period (*Krishna Paksha* in India). Then it grows back over another two weeks — the **waxing** period (*Shukla Paksha*). The full bright disc is the **full Moon** (*Purnima*); when nothing shows it is the **new Moon** (*Amavasya*). In between, when **more than half** the disc shows it is the **gibbous** phase, and when **less than half** shows it is the **crescent** phase. These changing shapes are the **phases of the Moon**, and the full cycle takes about a **month**.

slides.title: Locating the Moon
slides.intro: Knowing the phase tells you not just what the Moon looks like, but where and when to look for it.

slides.title: Full Moon rises as the Sun sets
slides.body: On a **full Moon** day the Moon is nearly **opposite the Sun** — when the Sun rises in the East, the Moon is almost setting in the West. As its bright part shrinks on later mornings, the Moon moves **closer to the Sun** in the sky: at half circle it is overhead at sunrise, and the crescent sits closer still. So a **waxing** Moon is easiest to spot at **sunset**, a **waning** Moon at **sunrise**, and the Moon always rises and sets at **different times than the Sun**.

slides.title: Reading the Moon's phase to find it
slides.leftBody: Bright part growing, drifting away from the Sun. Easiest to spot at **sunset** in the western sky.
slides.rightBody: Bright part shrinking, creeping back toward the Sun. Easiest to spot at **sunrise** in the eastern sky.

slides.title: The Moon does not rise when the Sun sets
slides.body: Many people believe the Moon rises as the Sun sets — but that isn't true. Check the moonrise time in a local newspaper or on the **Positional Astronomy Centre** website for several days, and you'll find the Moon rises about **50 minutes later each day**. Sometimes moonrise falls in the afternoon (around 2:00–4:00 p.m.), so you can spot the Moon in the **eastern daytime sky** — just as Meera did.

slides.title: Making sense of our observations
slides.intro: The Moon itself never changes shape — only what we see of it does. A ball, a stick, and a lamp will show us why.

slides.title: Half the Moon is always sunlit
slides.body: The Moon emits no light of its own — it shines by **reflecting sunlight**, so the half facing the Sun is always **illuminated** and the other half stays **non-illuminated**. But as the Moon revolves around Earth, the lit half is **not always the half facing us** — so from Earth we see only the lit portion that happens to point our way, and it is rarely a full circle. Let us model exactly that.

slides.title: A ball, a stick, and a lamp
slides.purpose: To understand how the lit portion we see changes, we model it: your head is the **Earth**, a lamp is the **Sun**, and a ball on a stick is the **Moon**.
steps: Set up — push a stick into a small soft ball; in a dark place, have a lamp shine on you from a few metres away
Hold — raise the ball at arm's length, slightly above your head, with the ball toward the lamp (position E)
Turn — rotate slowly anti-clockwise through positions A to H, keeping your eye on the ball each time
slides.observe: With the ball **opposite the lamp** (position A) you face the **entire lit side** — a full Moon. With the ball **toward the lamp** (position E) you face the **dark side** — a new Moon. In between, the dividing line looks **curved**, giving the same gibbous and crescent shapes as the real Moon.

slides.title: Why the Moon's shape changes
slides.caption: Drag through the month: the Sun always lights half the Moon, but from Earth we see a different slice of that lit half each night.

slides.title: Phases are not Earth's shadow
slides.body: As the Moon revolves once around Earth in about a month, the slice of its lit half facing us keeps changing — **full Moon**, then waning to **new Moon**, then waxing back. It is a common mistake to think this comes from **Earth's shadow** falling on the Moon. It does not — phases arise from the changing **orientation** of the Sun, Moon, and Earth. Earth's shadow on the Moon causes a **lunar eclipse** instead, which is rare because the Moon's orbit is slightly **tilted**, so the shadow usually misses.

slides.title: How did calendars come into existence?
slides.intro: The changing phases of the Moon are a natural periodic event — and so are day, season, and year. How did people turn these cycles into calendars?

slides.title: The mean solar day
slides.body: The Sun appears to **rise in the east and set in the west** because the **Earth rotates on its axis** — this natural cycle is the foundation of the **day**. The average time from the Sun's highest point one day to its highest point the next is 24 hours, the **mean solar day**. The Sun is highest when an object's **shadow is shortest**.

slides.kicker: ACTIVITY 11.3 · LET US MEASURE A DAY!
slides.title: Measure a day with a shadow
slides.purpose: The day is our basic unit of time — but is it really 24 hours? We measure it ourselves using nothing but a stick and its shadow.
steps: Fix — plant a 1 m stick vertically on flat sunlit ground
Mark — from 11:00 a.m., mark a dot at the shadow's tip every minute until about 1:10 p.m.
Identify — find when the shadow was shortest and note that time in a table; repeat over the next few days
slides.observe: The shortest-shadow time falls at nearly the **same moment each day** (around 12:20). The difference between two consecutive days — the **solar day** — comes out to almost exactly **24 hours**, confirming the day as a natural unit of time.

slides.title: Day, month, year
slides.body: Three regular cycles in the sky give us our three units of time — each tied to a different motion:
chips: Day — Earth rotates once on its axis
Month — Moon revolves once around Earth (~29.5 days)
Year — Earth revolves once around the Sun (~365¼ days)

slides.title: Lunar calendars
slides.intro: Twelve cycles of the Moon nearly fill one cycle of seasons — the oldest way to count a year.

slides.title: Twelve lunar months
slides.body: Ancient people noticed that about **12 cycles of the Moon's phases** fit into one cycle of seasons — so **lunar calendars** arose, with the day as the smallest unit, a month of nearly **29.5 days**, and a lunar year of 12 lunar months. But the lunar year runs only about **354 days** while seasons repeat in roughly 365, so in a lunar calendar the **seasons slowly drift** out of step with the months.

slides.title: Solar calendars
slides.intro: To keep the year locked to the seasons — important for farming — people turned to the Sun.

slides.title: The Gregorian calendar and the leap year fix
slides.body: Knowing when seasons arrive matters for **agriculture**, so **solar calendars** synchronise the year with the seasons. The widely used **Gregorian calendar** is solar, with months adjusted to add up to **365 days** — which is why some have 30, some 31, and February 28. But Earth takes nearly an extra **quarter day** to orbit the Sun, so a **leap day** (February 29) is added every fourth year. A finer rule skips the leap year in century years unless divisible by 400 — like 1600 and 2000 — keeping the calendar matched to the seasons over centuries.

slides.translation: Through years of careful sky-watching, Indians tracked the Sun's northward drift (Dec–June) as *Uttarayan* and its southward drift (June–Dec) as *Dakshinayan*. The *Surya Siddhanta* even noted that the stars of Capricorn (*Makar* in India) sat behind the Sun at the winter solstice in ancient times.

slides.title: Luni-solar calendars
slides.intro: What if a calendar followed the Moon for its months but still stayed in step with the seasons?

slides.title: Adding an extra month
slides.body: A **luni-solar calendar** uses the Moon's phases for counting days and months, but adjusts to keep step with the seasons. The 12 lunar months fall short of the solar year by nearly **11 days**, so every 2–3 years the gap grows close to a full month — and an extra month, the **Adhika Maasa** (intercalary month), is inserted. This keeps the lunar cycle and solar year aligned. Many Indian calendars work this way.

slides.title: How the world counts the year
The Indian National Calendar
slides.intro: India keeps its own official solar calendar alongside the Gregorian one.

slides.title: A year that begins on 22 March
slides.body: The **Indian National Calendar** is a **solar** calendar of 365 days, used for official purposes alongside the Gregorian. Its year begins on **22 March** — the day after the spring equinox — and its months, named from traditional Indian calendars, have 30 or 31 days. In leap years a day is added to **Chaitra**, the first month, and the year begins on 21 March. It follows the principles of the **Surya Siddhanta**; the **Calendar Reform Committee**, chaired by astrophysicist **Meghnad Saha**, adopted it from 1 Chaitra 1878 Saka (22 March 1956 CE).

slides.title: Are festivals related to astronomical phenomena?
slides.intro: Many Indian festivals are tied to the sky — which is exactly why their Gregorian dates wander from year to year.

slides.title: Why festivals shift each year
slides.body: Many Indian festivals follow the **Moon's phases**: *Diwali* on the new Moon of *Kartika*, *Holi* on the full Moon of *Phalguna*, *Buddha Purnima* on the full Moon of *Vaisakha*. Because these lunar dates don't line up with the solar Gregorian calendar, the festivals **fall on different dates each year**. For luni-solar festivals the shift stays under a month (the Adhika Maasa corrects it), but purely lunar ones like *Eid-ul-Fitr* drift further.

slides.title: The Rashtriya Panchang
slides.body: Festival dates depend on the exact **lunar phase at sunrise** — and since sunrise comes earlier in eastern India than in the west, dates can shift by a day across regions. To keep the country uniform, the **Positional Astronomy Centre** annually publishes the **Rashtriya Panchang**, a detailed calculation of the positions of the **Sun and Moon** for a central location in India, giving the Government advance dates for declaring holidays.

slides.title: Why do we launch artificial satellites in space?
slides.intro: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite — but it is no longer alone up there.

slides.title: Satellites that serve us
slides.body: The Moon is Earth's **natural satellite**. Besides it, **artificial satellites** sent up by many countries orbit the Earth — most about **800 km up**, taking roughly **100 minutes** per orbit, and appearing as tiny specks of steady light moving fast across the night sky. They help with **communication, navigation, weather monitoring, disaster management,** and scientific research.

slides.title: ISRO's missions
slides.body: The **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** has launched many satellites. The **Cartosat** series maps India to improve maps, plan cities, and manage disasters — feeding platforms like *Bhuvan*. **AstroSat** observes stars and other celestial objects. India's missions also include **Chandrayaan 1, 2, and 3** to the Moon, **Aditya-L1** to study the Sun, and **Mangalyaan** to Mars. ISRO even lets students build small satellites such as AzaadiSat, InspireSat-1, and Jugnu.

slides.title: Spot an artificial satellite
slides.purpose: Satellites are visible to the naked eye if you know what to look for — this is a night-sky watching activity like the ones before.
steps: Go — just before sunrise or after sunset, with an adult, find a spot with a clear view, free of trees or tall buildings
Look — search for a point of light with steady, non-flickering brightness moving very fast across the sky
Use — a mobile app or website to find which satellites pass over your location and when
slides.observe: Unlike a twinkling star or a slow-blinking aircraft, a satellite shows a **steady glow** and glides **smoothly and quickly** across the sky — its motion, like the Moon's and the Sun's, is **periodic**.

slides.title: The sky has always kept our time
slides.subtitle: From a daytime crescent over Ahmedabad to the Panchang, the Saka calendar, and ISRO's satellites — every clock and calendar we use began with patient, careful watching of the skies.
